objective: By the end of this lesson you can describe the seven teaching method items the PTS lists (material organization, the lecture, cooperative or group learning, guided discussion, demonstration-performance, computer-based training and scenario-based training) in the current AIH's terms, say what each one is, how it runs, when it fits and when it does not, and show how you would use each one in instrument training.
why: A flight instructor applicant must receive and log ground training on the fundamentals of instructing, including lesson planning and classroom training techniques, unless already an instructor or a qualified teacher [[60:340|14 CFR 61.185(a)(1)]] [[60:340|14 CFR 61.185(b)]]. The AIH says an instructor's success is determined to a large degree by the ability to organize material and to select and use a teaching method suited to the lesson [[25:125|AIH 5-22]], and that an effective instructor normally uses a combination of methods [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]. On a flight instructor practical test, the PTS expects your explanations to follow the AIH, including scenario-based lessons [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]], and tells the evaluator to test application and correlation with scenario-based questions [[FAA-S-8081-9E:14|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]], so you must be able to pick and defend a method for a real learner.

warmup: Think first: you will teach an evening ground lesson on the ILS to three instrument learners, and the next morning fly with one of them under the hood in a training device and then the airplane. Which teaching method would you use for each part of those two days, and what would make you switch methods partway through?

key_terms.def: The plan that leads learners logically toward the goal. A lesson is traditionally organized as introduction (attention, motivation, overview), development and conclusion [[25:112|AIH 5-9]] [[25:113|AIH 5-10]].
An oral presentation planned and delivered so learners take some part and are directed toward the desired outcomes. Aviation instructors favor it [[25:114|AIH 5-11]].
An instructional strategy that organizes learners into small groups so they can work together to maximize their own and each other's learning [[25:210|AIH G-2]].
A method used to make sure learners have correctly received and interpreted information. Learners need some background first, and the instructor keeps control of the discussion [[25:116|AIH 5-13]].
In a guided discussion, a question that opens up an area for discussion and gets it started [[25:212|AIH G-4]]. It should usually begin with how or why [[25:118|AIH 5-15]].
A summary given after the discussion of each learning outcome to bring ideas together, help the transition and show how the discussion supported the objective [[25:118|AIH 5-15]].

A method in which the instructor first shows the learner the correct way to perform an activity and then has the learner attempt it [[25:210|AIH G-2]]. It is based on the principle that people learn by doing [[25:124|AIH 5-21]].
The demonstration-performance method applied to flight instruction, with the key transition step learner tells, instructor does [[25:176|AIH 9-6]] [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
Any type of education that involves an electronic component, such as the Internet, a network, a stand-alone computer, CD/DVDs, video conferencing, websites or e-mail [[25:211|AIH G-3]].
The use of the computer as a training device; also called computer-based instruction (CBI), and the terms are synonymous [[25:210|AIH G-2]].
The AIH's chosen term for the educational use of the computer: a personal computer coupled with multimedia software to create a training device [[25:122|AIH 5-19]].
A training method that uses a highly structured script of real-world experiences to address aviation training objectives in an operational environment [[25:214|AIH G-6]].

chunks.title: Seven methods, and where the current AIH teaches them

body.p: This lesson follows the seven items the PTS lists for the Teaching Methods Task [[FAA-S-8081-9E:24|PTS I.D]]. The PTS references the older FAA-H-8083-9; this lesson teaches from the current 9B and maps the old names to the new ones. The CFI lesson FI.I.C covers the same AIH sections briefly for the CFI ACS, and the Teaching Process lesson FOI.I.C covers preparing, presenting, applying and assessing a lesson. Here each method gets four things: what it is, its steps or parts, when it fits and when it does not, and an instrument training example.

The AIH lists today's training delivery methods as lecture, discussion, guided discussion, problem based, group learning, demonstration-performance and e-learning. In a typical lesson an effective instructor normally uses a combination, choosing which method best conveys the information and when [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]. Bob, the maintenance instructor who opens the chapter, lectures on weight and balance, has small groups solve the first problem while they discuss it, reviews the steps, then has each learner solve another problem alone [[25:104|AIH 5-1]].

The 9B text uses electronic learning (e-learning) as the umbrella term and says that, of the many terms for the educational use of the computer, it will use 'computer-assisted learning' [[25:121|AIH 5-18]] [[25:122|AIH 5-19]]. Answer with the 9B words, and show the examiner you know the old one.

body.p: The AIH's verdict on the whole Task: lecture and demonstration-performance usually work well, but knowing the other methods prepares you for more situations, and sometimes a less-used tool is exactly the one needed [[25:125|AIH 5-22]].

check.q: An examiner asks which single teaching method you would use for an instrument ground lesson. Why is naming just one a weak answer?
check.a: The AIH says an effective instructor normally uses a combination of methods in a typical lesson and decides which method best conveys each part and when [[25:113|AIH 5-10]], as Bob does with a lecture followed by group work and then individual work [[25:104|AIH 5-1]].

chunks.title: Material organization I: from the course to the lesson

body.p: Organization starts above the single lesson. After setting objectives and standards, the instructor makes a plan of action that leads learners through the course in a logical way toward the goal, such as an instrument rating, and a systematic plan requires an appropriate training syllabus [[25:112|AIH 5-9]]. A syllabus outlines a course of several lessons, each with objectives and completion standards; a lesson plan is the detailed plan for one lesson and includes the organization of the material being covered [[25:107|AIH 5-4]]. The instructor's main concern is usually organizing a block of training with integrated lesson plans [[25:112|AIH 5-9]].

**Blocks of learning.** The instructor identifies the blocks that make up the total objective and checks that each is an integral part of the structure, because extraneous blocks are expensive frills, especially in flight [[25:146|AIH 7-2]]. Blocks should be units of learning that can be measured and evaluated, not a sequence of periods of instruction [[25:146|AIH 7-2]]. Humans learn from the simple to the complex: a learner should master normal landings before short-field and soft-field landings [[25:146|AIH 7-2]].

**Know the learner first.** Knowing the learner's aviation background lets you plan blocks that build on what the learner already knows [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]. Under part 61 the syllabus is a guide: the order of training can and should be changed to suit the learner's progress, but when you depart from it, consider how the blocks relate [[25:147|AIH 7-3]].

**An instrument example.** The IFH's Instrument Training Lesson Guide is built this way. Its lessons are arranged in a logical learning sequence using the building-block technique, each with ground training matched to the flight portion, and the instructor should brief the objective of each lesson and how it will be accomplished, then debrief the learner's performance [[23:342|IFH B-1]]. Attitude instrument flying comes in Lesson 4, partial panel operations in Lesson 6 and recovery from unusual attitudes in Lesson 7 [[23:342|IFH B-1]] [[23:343|IFH B-2]].

callout.text: Application: when a learner brings a strong background, look for blocks you can build on instead of repeating them. The AIH's example is a helicopter pilot moving to airplanes who understands speed control but may not know how to achieve it in an airplane [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]. An instrument learner who already flies a glass panel VFR may need less time on reading the displays and more on the cross-check.

check.q: Your learner keeps struggling with partial panel in Lesson 6, and the syllabus says unusual attitudes come next. What does the AIH say about changing the order?
check.a: Under part 61 the order can and should be changed to fit the learner, but you must consider how the blocks relate. The AIH's example delays short-field landings and reviews slow flight so the learner can do well and regain confidence [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]. Application: go back to a block the learner can succeed at, such as the full panel cross-check, before adding more.

chunks.title: Material organization II: introduction, development and conclusion

body.p: The traditional organization of a lesson plan is introduction, development and conclusion [[25:112|AIH 5-9]]. The introduction sets the stage for everything to come and has three elements: attention, motivation and an overview [[25:112|AIH 5-9]].

head: Part
What the AIH says
Instrument example (Application)
rows: Attention
Focus each learner on the lesson with a story, video clip, question or joke that relates to the subject. A story or joke unrelated to the subject distracts [[25:112|AIH 5-9]]
Open a partial panel lesson by asking what the learner would do if the attitude indicator failed in cloud
Motivation

Specific reasons the content matters, which ensures readiness (Thorndike's law of readiness). Give examples of someone applying it, or mention an upcoming assessment; appeal to each learner personally [[25:112|AIH 5-9]]

Tie it to the learner's own planned IFR trips, and note that the instrument rating test requires a nonprecision approach without the primary flight instruments, as the PTS points out [[FAA-S-8081-9E:16|PTS Emphasis on Partial Panel Skills]] [[FAA-S-ACS-8C:29|IR ACS IR.VII.D.S2]]

A clear, concise statement of the objective and key ideas: a road map. A good visual aid helps show the path [[25:112|AIH 5-9]]
'Today: the failure, your scan without it, then a full approach'

body.p: **Four ways to develop the main points** [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]:

bullets: **Past to present:** time order, best when history matters, as in tracing the development of radio navigation systems [[25:113|AIH 5-10]].

**Simple to complex:** lead from simple facts to the concept, and leave out less important information at first, because less information at first is easier to absorb [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]. The IFH lesson guide puts attitude instrument flying (Lesson 4) before partial panel operations (Lesson 6) [[23:342|IFH B-1]] [[23:343|IFH B-2]].
**Known to unknown:** start from something the learner knows. The AIH's own example is an instrument one: discuss the magnetic compass before gyroscopic heading indicators [[25:113|AIH 5-10]].

**Most frequently used to least used:** start with what everyone uses. Even when an aircraft has a computerized navigation system, begin with the basics of navigation, since all pilots use them [[25:113|AIH 5-10]].

body.p: **Transitions.** Subordinate points should lead naturally from one to the next, and meaningful transitions keep learners aware of where they have been and where they are going, which helps them sort and remember the information [[25:113|AIH 5-10]].

The same three-part shape appears under other names: the lecture runs introduction, body and summary [[25:113|AIH 5-10]], and the guided discussion runs introduction, discussion and conclusion [[25:117|AIH 5-14]]. In flight, a physical skill is usually explained in the step-by-step order used to perform it; known to unknown works when it builds on earlier skills, and simple to complex when teaching more than one skill at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

check.q: You finish a holding lesson by starting on DME arcs 'since we have five minutes left'. What did you break?
check.a: The conclusion should retrace the lesson's important elements and relate them to the objective. New ideas should not be introduced in the conclusion because they are likely to confuse the learners [[25:113|AIH 5-10]].

chunks.title: The lecture method: kinds and preparation

body.p: **What it is.** In the lecture method the instructor delivers knowledge to learners who are more or less silent participants. Lectures are best used to convey a general understanding of a subject, and generally run introduction, body and a summary of the main points [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]. They may introduce new subjects, summarize ideas, show relationships between theory and practice and reemphasize main points; they suit small or large groups and combine with other methods [[25:114|AIH 5-11]].

head: Kind of lecture
How it works
rows: Illustrated talk
The speaker relies heavily on visual aids to convey ideas [[25:114|AIH 5-11]]
Briefing
A concise array of facts; listeners do not expect elaboration of supporting material [[25:114|AIH 5-11]]
Formal lecture
The purpose is to inform, persuade or entertain, with little or no verbal participation by learners [[25:114|AIH 5-11]]
Teaching lecture
Planned and delivered so learners take some part, directing them toward the desired outcomes [[25:114|AIH 5-11]]
Informal lecture
Includes active learner participation, achieved with questions, in a friendly, relaxed atmosphere; the instructor still plans and presents the major portion [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]

body.p: **The teaching lecture** is favored by aviation instructors because it allows some active participation. Its feedback is much harder to read than in demonstration-performance or guided discussion, so develop a keen eye for facial expressions, how learners take notes and their apparent interest, and adjust the lesson [[25:114|AIH 5-11]].
**Preparing it.** Plan in four steps [[25:114|AIH 5-11]]:

bullets: Establish the objective and desired outcomes.
Research the subject.
Organize the material.
Plan productive classroom activities.

body.p: Support points with examples, comparisons, statistics, testimony and personal experience. Then rehearse to build confidence and smooth out notes and aids, ideally with another instructor watching as a critic [[25:114|AIH 5-11]].

callout.text: Application: an evening ground lesson on the ILS is a natural teaching lecture. The AIH's integrated ILS example starts exactly here: knowledge of ILS design and the associated flight operations taught through ground and classroom training, before the simulator and the airplane [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]. Plan a classroom activity for the middle, such as having learners find the parts of the approach on a chart.

check.q: What kind of lecture is a two-minute rundown of weather and NOTAMs before a training flight, and why?
check.a: A briefing: the speaker presents a concise array of facts, and listeners do not expect elaboration of supporting material [[25:114|AIH 5-11]] [[25:209|AIH G-1]].

chunks.title: Delivering a lecture, and when it fits

body.p: **Language.** Use simple words, define every technical term, and choose specific words over general ones: 'a leak in the fuel line' says more than 'discrepancy'. Vary tone and pace, and use sentences of short and medium length [[25:115|AIH 5-12]].

**Delivery.** A good teaching lecture is extemporaneous: you speak from a mental or written outline, but do not read or memorize the material. If puzzled faces show a point did not land, you can elaborate until reactions show understanding; this style reflects your enthusiasm, is more flexible and is likely to hold interest [[25:115|AIH 5-12]]. Notes ensure accuracy and jog the memory; use them sparingly and unobtrusively, but make no effort to hide them [[25:115|AIH 5-12]].

head: The lecture fits when
Watch out, because
rows: You must instruct a large group [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]
It gives no precise measure of how well learners understood [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]
Learners lack the time or references to find the information themselves [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]
Retention drops off significantly after the first 10-15 minutes, and improves at the end [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]
You need to present many ideas in a short time [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]
It does not foster motor skills, which must be perfected by hands-on practice [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]
Learners with varied backgrounds need a common understanding of essential principles and facts [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]
It needs considerable skill in speaking [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]

body.p: A brief introductory lecture can give direction and purpose to a demonstration or prepare learners for a discussion [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]. The fix for the retention drop is built into the method: an instructor who introduces some form of active learner participation in the middle of a lecture greatly increases retention [[25:116|AIH 5-13]].

callout.text: A lecture cannot build the instrument cross-check. Motor skills must be perfected through hands-on practice [[25:116|AIH 5-13]], which is what demonstration-performance is for [[25:124|AIH 5-21]]. Application: lecture the why of partial panel flying, then teach the scan in a training device or the airplane.

check.q: Twenty-five minutes into your lecture on IFR alternates, faces go blank. What does the AIH suggest?
check.a: Retention drops significantly after the first 10-15 minutes; bringing in active learner participation in the middle greatly increases retention [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]. The extemporaneous style also lets you expand a point when you see puzzled faces [[25:115|AIH 5-12]].

body.p: **What it is.** Cooperative or group learning organizes learners into small groups who work together to maximize understanding [[25:124|AIH 5-21]], their own and each other's [[25:210|AIH G-2]]. Research indicates better test scores, higher self-esteem, improved social skills and greater comprehension. Perhaps its most significant characteristic is that it continually requires active participation [[25:124|AIH 5-21]].

**Conditions and controls.** Success depends on them. Begin planning early: decide what the group is to learn and be able to do on its own, and use clear, specific objectives for the knowledge or abilities learners must acquire and then demonstrate on their own [[25:124|AIH 5-21]]. The AIH lists these conditions and controls [[25:124|AIH 5-21]]:

bullets: Small, heterogeneous groups.
Clear, complete instructions: what to do, in what order, with what materials, and what learners will do as evidence of mastery.
Learners see the targeted objectives as their own, personal objectives.
The opportunity for learner success.
Learner access to and comprehension of the required information.
Sufficient time for learning.
Individual accountability.
Recognition and rewards for group success.
Time after the group task to reflect systematically on how they worked together as a team.

body.p: **Types and your role.** Collaborative, learner-led, instructor-led and working group strategies are all types of group learning. The leader or instructor serves as a coach or facilitator, stepping in as needed to keep the group on track and to get everyone to participate [[25:124|AIH 5-21]]. Many of the AIH's guided discussion planning suggestions also apply to cooperative learning [[25:117|AIH 5-14]].

**When it fits and when it does not.** It is a strong way to reinforce a lecture, as Bob does [[25:104|AIH 5-1]], and cooperative learning is one of the AIH's strategies for teaching higher order thinking skills [[25:57|AIH 3-6]]. It needs a group, though. For a single learner, the AIH notes that collaborative problem-solving can be modified for one-on-one instruction: you give the learner the problem and offer limited help as the learner solves it [[25:121|AIH 5-18]].

callout.text: Application, instrument ground school: mix experience levels in each group. Give each group one approach chart, a list of what to brief in a set order, and a time limit; give each member one part to brief. Then have each learner brief a different chart alone, Bob's pattern of a group problem followed by an individual one [[25:104|AIH 5-1]], and close with a few minutes on how the teams worked [[25:124|AIH 5-21]].

check.q: In your group chart exercise, one strong learner does all the briefing while the others watch. Which condition did your plan miss, and how do you fix it?
check.a: Individual accountability [[25:124|AIH 5-21]]. Give each member a part to brief, and finish with each learner working a chart alone, as Bob has each learner solve a problem independently [[25:104|AIH 5-1]].

chunks.title: Guided discussion I: what it is, and the questions that drive it

body.p: **Discussion and guided discussion.** The 9B has both. The discussion method opens with a short lecture, then instructor-learner and learner-learner discussion; the instructor keeps it focused, comments on disagreements, gets everyone to take part, summarizes, and keeps their own talking to a minimum [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]. The **guided discussion method** is used to make sure the learner has correctly received and interpreted the information. Learners need some knowledge first, from reading or a short lecture, and the instructor maintains control. It works in the classroom and in preflight and postflight briefings [[25:116|AIH 5-13]].

Its goal is to draw out what the learner knows: the greater the participation, the more effective the learning. Treat everyone impartially, encourage questions, be patient and tactful, comment on all responses to reinforce an objective, and never use sarcasm [[25:116|AIH 5-13]].
**Questions do the work.** Learning in a guided discussion is achieved through the skillful use of questions [[25:117|AIH 5-14]]:

bullets: A **lead-off question** opens an area for discussion [[25:117|AIH 5-14]].
A **follow-up question** guides it: to get a fuller explanation, or to bring the discussion back to a point it strayed from [[25:117|AIH 5-14]].
You may answer a question with a question, directed back to the asker or to another participant [[25:117|AIH 5-14]].

Avoid questions answered by a short fact or yes or no. Ask open-ended, thought-provoking ones; since most aviation training is at the understanding level or higher, questions should require learners to grasp concepts, explain similarities and differences, and infer cause and effect [[25:117|AIH 5-14]].

body.p: Lead-off questions should usually begin with how or why. 'Why does an aircraft normally require a longer takeoff run at Denver than at New Orleans?' starts a discussion of density, engine efficiency and temperature; 'Denver or New Orleans?' gets one word [[25:118|AIH 5-15]].

head: Weak question
Better lead-off
What the learner should reach
rows: 'Do you scan the standby instruments?'
'Why do pilots flying a PFD tend to leave the standby instruments out of their scan?'
The PFD's high reliability and the standby instruments' position lead to omission, yet they must be monitored to detect failures [[23:161|IFH 6-28]]
'Is the slip/skid indicator important?'
'How does leaving the slip/skid indicator out of the cross-check show up when you roll out of a turn?'
It is one of the most commonly omitted instruments, and omitting it sacrifices coordination [[23:161|IFH 6-28]]
'Did you trim?'
'Why does an untrimmed airplane make the rest of your cross-check harder?'
A trimmed airplane lets the pilot relax control pressure and divert attention without the attitude changing; poor trim is one of the most common errors in instrument students [[23:153|IFH 6-20]]

check.q: Your planned lead-off is 'Is partial panel harder than full panel?' What is wrong with it, and how do you fix it?
check.a: It can be answered yes or no. Ask open-ended questions that usually begin with how or why so they start a discussion [[25:117|AIH 5-14]] [[25:118|AIH 5-15]], for example 'Why is partial panel flying harder than full panel?'

chunks.title: Guided discussion II: planning it, running it, and using it one-on-one

body.p: **Planning** is like planning a lecture [[25:117|AIH 5-14]] [[25:118|AIH 5-15]]:

bullets: Select a topic learners know something about. Unless they have knowledge to exchange, they cannot reach the outcomes, so assign background work if needed [[25:117|AIH 5-14]].
State the specific objective at the understanding level of learning; the desired learning outcomes stem from it [[25:117|AIH 5-14]].
Research the topic, and earmark well-organized background reading for learners [[25:117|AIH 5-14]].
Organize the main and subordinate points logically in three parts: introduction (attention, motivation, overview), discussion and conclusion [[25:117|AIH 5-14]].
Plan at least one lead-off question for each desired learning outcome [[25:118|AIH 5-15]].

body.p: **Learner preparation** is your job. Keep learners aware of the objective. If you had no chance to assign prework, give a brief general survey of the topic in the introduction, because learners normally should not be asked to discuss a subject without some background [[25:118|AIH 5-15]].

**Running it.** Create a relaxed, informal atmosphere in which each learner feels free, and responsible, to contribute. Open with a prepared lead-off question and give learners time to think; harder questions need more time, and puzzled faces mean you should rephrase. Listen, compare what you hear with the responses you anticipated, and use how and why follow-ups to steer toward the objective. After each learning outcome, give an **interim summary** to bring ideas together and make the transition; it can also keep the group on the subject or move the discussion to another member [[25:118|AIH 5-15]]. **Conclude** by summarizing and tying the points to practical use, such as a density altitude accident at the end of a density altitude discussion; if some areas were not understood, cover them again [[25:118|AIH 5-15]].

**When it fits.** Discussion lets learners learn from you and from each other; open-ended questions lead to risk management and ADM, and 'What if?' calls for higher order thinking [[25:119|AIH 5-16]]. It works well in groups but can be modified for one-on-one instruction: as the learner grows, the learner should lead the postflight review while you guide with targeted questions [[25:119|AIH 5-16]]. **When it does not:** learners with no background cannot reach the outcomes [[25:117|AIH 5-14]], and its objective sits at the understanding level [[25:117|AIH 5-14]], so physical skills still need a method built on practice [[25:124|AIH 5-21]].

callout.text: Application, a postflight guided discussion after a partial panel approach. Lead-off: 'How did your cross-check change once the attitude indicator was covered?' Follow-up: 'Why did the altitude wander in the turn to final?' Interim summary, then: 'What if this happened in cloud with no instructor aboard?' Let the learner do most of the talking [[25:116|AIH 5-13]] [[25:119|AIH 5-16]].

check.q: Your learner arrives for an evening guided discussion on icing without having done the reading. What do you do?
check.a: Learners normally should not discuss a subject without some background. When there was no chance for prework, give a brief general survey of the topic in the introduction [[25:118|AIH 5-15]], then continue with the discussion.

body.p: **What it is.** Demonstration-performance is best for mastering mental or physical skills that require practice, and it is based on the principle that people learn by doing: learners watch the skill and then try to reproduce it. It suits the flight instructor teaching piloting skills [[25:124|AIH 5-21]]. Chapter 9 calls it very effective for kinesthetic skills and valuable for procedures and maneuvers [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. Early in the lesson, identify the most important outcomes, explain and demonstrate the steps, and let learners practice each step [[25:124|AIH 5-21]].

Chapter 5 divides the method into **five phases** [[25:124|AIH 5-21]]. Chapter 9, written for flight instructors, lists **four**, because learner performance and instructor supervision are separate actions done at the same time [[25:175|AIH 9-5]] [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. Both are correct; know both.

head: Phase
What the AIH requires
Instrument example: pitch control in level flight
rows: Explanation

Clear, pertinent to the objective and based on what the learner knows; give the precise actions and the end result, and invite questions [[25:124|AIH 5-21]]. In flight training it happens before the flight: objectives, completion standards, a thorough preflight briefing and safety procedures, with the learner intellectually and psychologically ready [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]
On the ground, explain pitch changes of one-half, one and one-and-one-half bar widths on the attitude indicator [[23:164|IFH 7-3]], and brief how you will exchange the controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
Demonstration

Show the actions, and you may describe them at the same time. Leave out extraneous activity. If the demonstration departs from the explanation, acknowledge and explain it immediately [[25:125|AIH 5-22]] [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]
The IFH suggests an instructor pilot demonstrate the normal pitch corrections and compare the attitude indicator with the natural horizon [[23:164|IFH 7-3]]
Learner performance and instructor supervision

Concurrent. Allot enough time for meaningful activity and let the learner perform as soon as possible after the demonstration; in flight the learner may follow along on the controls, then try it with coaching [[25:125|AIH 5-22]]
Under the hood, the learner makes the same corrections while you coach
Evaluation

The learner works independently while you judge the performance against the way it was taught, which also shows how effective your instruction was [[25:125|AIH 5-22]]. Record it, tell the learner the progress made, give concrete suggestions, and avoid ending on a negative note [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]
The learner holds altitude alone; you compare the corrections with what you taught

check.q: During your demonstration of a level-off, turbulence knocks the altitude off from what you briefed. What does the AIH tell you to do?
check.a: If the demonstration deviates from the explanation, acknowledge and explain the deviation immediately [[25:125|AIH 5-22]] [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

chunks.title: Demonstration-performance II: telling-and-doing in the instrument airplane

body.p: In flight, the AIH applies the method as the **telling-and-doing technique**, with variations for flight instruction [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. Its key transition, learner tells and instructor does, comes between the second and third steps [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. The Learning Process lesson (FOI.I.A) lists the steps; here is how to use them under the hood.

bullets: **Instructor tells, instructor does.** A carefully planned demonstration with explanation of power settings, attitudes and other factors. It is the only step where the learner is passive. Demonstrate in the same order you explained, and exactly the way the learner should practice it, including safety procedures, because learners generally imitate the instructor. Avoid jargon the learner does not know [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

**Learner tells, instructor does.** The learner plays instructor. Freed from flying, the learner organizes the steps, and you can judge the learner's understanding. Because of primacy, make sure the learner gets it right the first time; a misunderstanding can be corrected before the learner is absorbed in controlling the aircraft [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

**Learner tells, learner does.** Application, where performance habits form. The learner thinks aloud, which focuses concentration and shows you whether an error comes from a misconception or a simple lack of motor skill. Use judgment about how much control to use, be ready to take over in hazardous maneuvers, avoid needless interruptions when progress is normal, and schedule more training if the objective is not met in the time allotted [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

body.p: **An instrument demonstration from the IFH.** An instructor pilot can demonstrate an excessive nose-down deviation and then the result of improper technique: a large, hurried pitch correction leads to overcontrolling, tension, erratic response and increasingly extreme control movements. The correct technique, slower and smoother, returns the airplane to the desired attitude more quickly [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]. As a rule of thumb, use a half bar width correction for altitude errors under 100 feet and an initial full bar width for errors over 100 feet [[23:165|IFH 7-4]].

**Positive exchange of flight controls** is especially critical during demonstration-performance. Brief the procedure before the flight; the AIH strongly recommends a positive three-step exchange [[25:178|AIH 9-8]], which the PTS spells out as 'You have the flight controls', 'I have the flight controls', 'You have the flight controls', with a visual check [[FAA-S-8081-9E:16|PTS Positive Exchange of Flight Controls]]. Always guard the controls and, when needed, take them and calmly announce 'I have the flight controls' [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

**Drill and practice** follows naturally. Based on the law of exercise, it predicts that connections are strengthened with practice: nobody masters crosswind landings in one flight. Give learners chances to practice, and direct the practice toward an objective [[25:125|AIH 5-22]].

callout.text: The PTS asks a CFII applicant to 'demonstrate and simultaneously explain' [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]]. The AIH's demonstration phase allows exactly that: the instructor demonstrates and may describe the actions simultaneously [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. Because the PTS also has the evaluator act as a student [[FAA-S-8081-9E:14|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]], expect to run telling-and-doing on the evaluator.

check.q: In the learner tells, learner does step, your learner describes the level-off steps in a different order from the one you taught, then flies them that way. What has the talking aloud told you, and what do you do?
check.a: That the error is a misconception, not a lack of motor skill; talking aloud makes that easy to tell [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Correct the sequence now, because faulty habits are difficult to correct and should be addressed as soon as possible [[25:126|AIH 5-23]].

chunks.title: Computer-based training I: e-learning and computer-assisted learning

body.p: **What it is now called.** E-learning has become the umbrella term for any education with an electronic component. It can be a stand-alone program that takes a learner from lecture to exam, or an interactive web-based course [[25:121|AIH 5-18]]. Within it, the AIH uses the term computer-assisted learning (CAL): a personal computer coupled with multimedia software to create a training device [[25:122|AIH 5-19]]. The glossary's computer-based training (CBT) is the use of the computer as a training device [[25:210|AIH G-2]].

**Strengths.** E-learning is time flexible, cost competitive, learner-centered, easily updated and accessible anytime and anywhere [[25:121|AIH 5-18]]. Good programs let learners feel in control of content and pace and explore on their own; the main advantages are less time spent on instruction and a higher level of mastery and retention. Distance learning connects learners and instructors who are apart [[25:122|AIH 5-19]]. CAL lets learners progress at a comfortable rate and at their own convenience; FAA test prep study guides are one form, and advanced programs change the presentation based on the learner's responses [[25:122|AIH 5-19]]. Its major advantage is that it is interactive: the computer responds in different ways depending on learner input [[25:122|AIH 5-19]].

**Your role does not go away.** The computer has no way of knowing when a learner is having difficulty, so monitoring and oversight are always the instructor's job; stay involved through close supervision, questions, examinations, quizzes or guided discussions [[25:122|AIH 5-19]]. With CAL you become a supportive facilitator with more one-on-one time, but CAL is still an add-on aid and you keep control of the learning environment [[25:129|AIH 5-26]] [[25:130|AIH 5-27]]. A more advanced use of computer-based training, such as a learning center monitored by an aide, involves less instructor control, so the responsible instructor must set procedures to make sure required training is done, since that instructor certifies competency [[25:130|AIH 5-27]].

Lack of peer interaction and personal feedback, depending on the type of e-learning [[25:122|AIH 5-19]]

Hard for the instructor to keep control; good programs can be hard to find; equipment, software and facilities cost money; users may not know a program well [[25:122|AIH 5-19]]
Improper or excessive use

Do not rely only on a software program on traffic patterns and landings and then expect the learner to fly them [[25:122|AIH 5-19]]. Learners who use electronic media extensively are generally not as well trained as those who get a balanced mix [[25:172|AIH 9-2]]
Test prep material
Emphasizes rote learning, the lowest level; it is a supplement to instructor-led training, not a stand-alone tool [[25:131|AIH 5-28]]
Online information
There is no guarantee that all of it is current or even accurate [[25:131|AIH 5-28]]

callout.text: Where it fits in the levels of learning: the AIH says the first three cognitive levels (knowledge, comprehension, application) are generally gained from ground school, reading, briefings or computer-based training, while the highest levels can be reached through SBT [[25:67|AIH 3-16]]. Interactive computer-based instruction often goes hand in hand with the flight syllabus, delivering academics just in time [[25:92|AIH 3-41]]. Application: let an online module carry the facts of IFR charts, then check understanding with your own guided discussion before the flight.

check.q: Your learner aced every module of an online instrument course. Why do you still question her in person?
check.a: The computer has no way of knowing when a learner is having difficulty; monitoring progress is always the instructor's job, through supervision, questions, quizzes or guided discussion [[25:122|AIH 5-19]]. Test-prep style material also stresses rote learning [[25:131|AIH 5-28]].

chunks.title: Computer-based training II: simulators and training devices in instrument training

body.p: E-learning includes flight training devices and simulators used from flight schools to the airlines and the military; flight schools may use desktop basic aviation training devices (BATDs), personal computer based advanced aviation training devices (AATDs) and flight training devices (FTDs) for part of the time a pilot needs for certificates and ratings [[25:121|AIH 5-18]].

body.p: **Instrument use.** The IFH says ground-based equipment, from a flight simulator to a BATD, is a valuable tool for developing the instrument cross-check and for learning procedures such as intercepting and tracking, holding patterns and instrument approaches, which are then refined in flight [[23:11|IFH viii]]. The AIH's integrated curriculum uses an ILS: knowledge in the classroom, then procedures, then practice of the psychomotor skills in the simulator, where the instructor demonstrates and teaches the approach; once the learner is proficient, training moves to the aircraft to verify proficiency [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]. The FAA recommends continuing in the simulator until the tasks are done successfully before trying them in the aircraft [[25:174|AIH 9-4]].

callout.text: Credit toward the instrument rating: a maximum of 10 hours of instrument time in a basic ATD or 20 hours in an advanced ATD may be credited if the device is FAA approved and authorized, an authorized instructor provides the time, and the FAA approved the training and tasks performed [[60:253|14 CFR 61.65(i)]]. Except under paragraph (h)(1), no more than 20 total hours in an FFS, FTD, ATD or a combination may be credited [[60:253|14 CFR 61.65(j)]]. Up to 30 hours in an FFS or FTD may count if completed under part 142 [[60:252|14 CFR 61.65(h)(1)]]. There is no limit on how much time may be logged in a device; the limits are on credit [[25:174|AIH 9-4]].

body.p: **Simulation, role-playing and games.** Simulation games put the learner in a character's shoes facing a real-world scenario, give a stake in the outcome and usually promote critical thinking, but not every aviation objective can be delivered this way [[25:123|AIH 5-20]]. Virtual reality has enormous potential but is expensive [[25:131|AIH 5-28]].

callout.text: A device is a tool, not an instructor. In the AIH's ILS example the instructor demonstrates and teaches the approach in the trainer [[25:174|AIH 9-4]], and the AIH calls the computer a valuable instructional aid [[25:122|AIH 5-19]]. Application: run demonstration-performance in the device exactly as you would in the airplane, including partial panel.

check.q: Your school's AATD has an FAA letter of authorization. Can your learner take the instrument practical test in it?
check.a: No. ATDs cannot be used for airman practical tests or type rating training requirements [[25:173|AIH 9-3]].

chunks.title: Scenario-based training I: what it is and what makes a good scenario

body.p: **What it is.** SBT uses a highly structured script of real-world experiences to address aviation training objectives in an operational environment, presenting realistic situations that let learners rehearse mentally and apply knowledge [[25:120|AIH 5-17]]. It is one of three types of problem-based instruction, with collaborative problem-solving and the case study [[25:120|AIH 5-17]]. SBT lies at the heart of higher order thinking skills: it presents tasks in an operational environment, correlates new information with previous knowledge, and introduces new information in a realistic context [[25:57|AIH 3-6]]. It can include initial, transition, upgrade, recurrent and special training [[25:120|AIH 5-17]].

**Why it matters.** Pilot decisions cause a significant percentage of all accidents and the majority of fatal ones, and SBT challenges the learner with a variety of scenarios to manage resources, use sound judgment and make timely decisions [[25:120|AIH 5-17]]. Flight learners trained with SBT show flying skills equal to or better than those trained only by maneuvers, and better decision-making [[25:110|AIH 5-7]]. FAA training emphasis has moved from a maneuvers-based standard to SBT [[25:100|AIH 4-7]].

**Start with a reason to fly.** For a flight instructor, a good scenario tells a story that begins with a reason to fly, because a pilot's decisions differ depending on the motivation to fly. The AIH's Mark is flying friends to a playoff game when, 15 miles out, he is down to 1,000 feet under lowering clouds in rain with 3 miles visibility [[25:120|AIH 5-17]].

body.p: **Freedom inside safe limits.** Know in advance which outcomes are positive and which are negative, and let the learner make good and poor decisions without jeopardizing safety [[25:120|AIH 5-17]]. That never means letting the learner make an unsafe decision or commit an unsafe act [[25:144|AIH 6-13]].

**Your role changes.** Orient learners to SBT, help them become confident planners and critical self-evaluators, diagnose difficulties, keep records and review continuously [[25:155|AIH 7-11]]. Turn planning and execution of the flight over to the learner as soon as possible; keep teaching skill maneuvers in the traditional way, but once the learner is making decisions, become a mentor and learning facilitator [[25:155|AIH 7-11]] [[25:143|AIH 6-12]]. Scenarios should be planned and led by the learner, except for the first flight or two [[25:57|AIH 3-6]].

check.q: Halfway through your scenario, the learner picks a reasonable alternate you had not planned for. Is the scenario broken?
check.a: No. A good scenario will not have one right answer [[25:120|AIH 5-17]]. You know the good and poor outcomes in advance and let the learner make decisions that fit the learner's experience, as long as nothing unsafe is allowed [[25:144|AIH 6-13]].

chunks.title: Scenario-based training II: building an instrument scenario lesson

body.p: The SBT lesson plan differs from the traditional one [[25:155|AIH 7-11]]. In the AIH example the learner plans an arrival at a specific nontowered airport, considering wind, arrival paths, airport information, communication, runways, patterns, courses of action and the unexpected, then makes the decisions in flight with guidance and feedback. A discussion follows: what was done, why, the consequences, other options, and how it applies at other airports. The learner can then detail a safe arrival at any nontowered airport in a variety of winds, not just fly one maneuver [[25:155|AIH 7-11]].

**Pre-scenario planning.** For a flight scenario, the instructor and learner set the scenario destination(s), the desired learning outcomes, the desired level of learner performance, and possible inflight scenario changes. A nonflight scenario uses a narrative of the task goal in place of the destination [[25:155|AIH 7-11]].

**Maneuvers still have a place.** SBT does not preclude maneuver-based training. Maneuvers that need repetition may still be taught in concentrated settings, and once learned they are integrated into realistic flight situations [[25:110|AIH 5-7]] [[25:154|AIH 7-10]]. Figure 7-8 adds that most learning solutions should use both traditional training and SBT, with boundaries around scenarios so the transitions are efficient [[25:157|AIH 7-13]].

**Local and learner-led.** SBT rests on situated cognition: knowledge cannot be fully understood apart from its context. The learner is responsible for planning the flight scenario from a menu of short cross-country flights developed by the training provider. Scenarios can be tailored to local weather and terrain, and are most effective when they replicate the environment learners will most likely meet [[25:157|AIH 7-13]].

**Assessing it.** Collaborative assessment (learner centered grading) is used to judge whether learning criteria were met during SBT: a learner self-assessment, then a detailed instructor assessment and a discussion comparing the two [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. The Figure 7-7 postflight review typically begins with the learner's self-critique [[25:156|AIH 7-12]]. The Critique and Evaluation lesson (FOI.I.E) goes deeper.

Figure 7-7 says the discussion typically begins with learner self-critique, and the instructor lets the learner solve the problems and draw conclusions [[25:156|AIH 7-12]]; collaborative assessment then compares the self-assessment with yours [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

chunks.title: Choosing the method: mismatches, and how the examiner tests it

body.p: Each teaching situation is unique, so the setting and purpose of the lesson decide which method to use [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]. A wrong choice wastes the learner's time and money, and some mismatches leave real gaps in an instrument pilot's skill or judgment.

body.p: **Match the learner, too.** Learners progress from simple to complex, so they need some information about a subject before they can think about it beyond rote learning [[25:57|AIH 3-6]]. As the learner becomes proficient with the fundamentals, emphasize ADM as the way to apply what has been learned [[25:126|AIH 5-23]].

**How it is tested.** The PTS NOTE for Area I has the evaluator select at least Tasks E, F and G and one other, so this Task may or may not be chosen [[FAA-S-8081-9E:23|PTS Area I NOTE]]. The PTS defines instructional knowledge as following the AIH's recommended procedures, including scenario-based lessons [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]], and tells evaluators to test application and correlation with scenario-based questions where possible [[FAA-S-8081-9E:14|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]]. The AIH notes that a flight instructor applicant usually flies with an instructor who role-plays the learner [[25:100|AIH 4-7]], and the PTS has the evaluator act as a student during selected maneuvers [[FAA-S-8081-9E:14|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]].

callout.text: Application: answer any method question in three beats: what the method is (in AIH words), why it fits this learner and lesson, and how you would run it, with one instrument example. Then say what would make you switch.

check.q: An examiner says: 'Your learner can recite partial panel procedures but loses control in the device. Which method next, and why?'
check.a: Demonstration-performance: it is for skills that need practice and rests on learning by doing [[25:124|AIH 5-21]], while lecture does not build motor skills [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]. The device is a good place for the cross-check [[23:11|IFH viii]], with the learner thinking aloud so you can tell misconception from motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
