scenario.title: The evening ground school and the morning flight
scenario.setup: You are a CFII at a small part 61 school. The chief instructor asks you to run three evening ground sessions for four instrument learners, then fly with one of them, Dana. Two of the others are newer private pilots, and one is a helicopter pilot adding an airplane instrument rating. Dana is a private pilot with 220 hours in the school's fixed-pitch airplane, which has a glass panel and standby instruments. The school has an FAA-approved AATD and an online instrument ground course the learners already use. Dana scored well on every online module, but in her first AATD session she chased altitude with big, hurried pitch corrections. Her goal is to fly herself to client meetings two hours away.

questions.q: How would you organize the first evening, on the ILS, and which methods would you mix?
questions.a: Open with attention, motivation and an overview [[25:112|AIH 5-9]], and develop from what they already know (known to unknown) [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]. A teaching lecture suits the background, giving learners with varied backgrounds a common understanding [[25:116|AIH 5-13]], with participation in the middle to protect retention [[25:116|AIH 5-13]], then group work [[25:124|AIH 5-21]]. The AIH's integrated ILS curriculum starts with exactly this classroom knowledge before the simulator and airplane [[25:174|AIH 9-4]].

questions.q: How do you set up the group work so that the helicopter pilot and the newer pilots all learn?
questions.a: Small, heterogeneous groups, clear and complete instructions, enough time, individual accountability, recognition for group success, and time to reflect on the teamwork [[25:124|AIH 5-21]]. Use the helicopter pilot's background by building on what he already knows [[25:147|AIH 7-3]].

questions.q: Dana aced the online modules. What do you make of that, and what do you do before flying?
questions.a: The computer cannot tell when a learner is struggling, so check her yourself with questions, quizzes or a guided discussion [[25:122|AIH 5-19]]. The AIH ties computer-based training to the first three cognitive levels and SBT to the highest [[25:67|AIH 3-16]]. Use how and why lead-off questions that require understanding [[25:117|AIH 5-14]] [[25:118|AIH 5-15]].

questions.q: How do you fix her pitch chasing?
questions.a: Demonstration-performance. Explain pitch changes in bar widths before the flight [[25:175|AIH 9-5]] [[23:164|IFH 7-3]], demonstrate the improper hurried correction and then the correct slow, smooth one [[23:165|IFH 7-4]], then move through learner tells, instructor does to learner tells, learner does [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. The AATD suits cross-check work [[23:11|IFH viii]], and the FAA recommends staying in the simulator until tasks are done successfully [[25:174|AIH 9-4]].

questions.q: Later in her training, how would you design a scenario-based flight for Dana?
questions.a: Begin with her real reason to fly [[25:120|AIH 5-17]]; set the destination, desired outcomes, desired performance and possible changes in advance [[25:155|AIH 7-11]]; tailor it to the local environment [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]; know the good and poor outcomes and allow nothing unsafe [[25:144|AIH 6-13]]; and start the postflight review with her self-critique [[25:156|AIH 7-12]].

questions.q: The examiner asks: why not do the whole course in the AATD and online?
questions.a: That would be improper or excessive use of e-learning [[25:122|AIH 5-19]]; learners who rely heavily on electronic media are generally not as well trained as those given a balanced mix [[25:172|AIH 9-2]]. ATDs cannot be used for the practical test [[25:173|AIH 9-3]], and instrument time credit in an AATD is capped at 20 hours [[60:253|14 CFR 61.65(i)]].

skills.do: Explain demonstration-performance aloud the way an examiner expects: what it is, both the five-phase (Chapter 5) and four-phase (Chapter 9) versions and why they differ, how telling-and-doing applies it in flight, and one instrument example from explanation to evaluation.
skills.practice: With a study partner, brief pitch control for level flight in bar widths [[23:164|IFH 7-3]], then run the four phases [[25:175|AIH 9-5]] [[25:176|AIH 9-6]] in a training device, with your partner acting as a learner who overcorrects [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]. Afterward, name the phase where you caught the error and say how you corrected it.

skills.do: Build and brief a scenario-based instrument lesson: the reason to fly, the pre-scenario planning items, the hazards and planned changes, the safety boundaries, and how the postflight review will run.
skills.practice: Fill in the Figure 7-7 headings [[25:156|AIH 7-12]] for a real trip from your home airport, add the pre-scenario planning items [[25:155|AIH 7-11]], and check it against the AIH's traits of a good scenario [[25:120|AIH 5-17]] [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]. Brief it in under five minutes to another applicant, then lead a postflight review that starts with their self-critique.

quiz.q: You are planning an instrument ground lesson on heading indicators. Which opening does the AIH give as its own example of known to unknown?
options: Start with the history of radio navigation aids
Start with the magnetic compass, then gyro indicators
Start with the glass displays, then move to the older round gauges
Start with indicator failures, then normal use
quiz.why: The AIH's known-to-unknown example begins a heading indicator lesson with the magnetic compass before gyroscopic indicators [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]. Tracing the history of radio navigation is its past-to-present example, a different pattern [[25:113|AIH 5-10]].

quiz.q: What belongs in the conclusion of a lesson?
options: A short new topic to use up whatever time is left
The next lesson's new material, in detail
A review of key points tied to the objective
An unrelated story to end the lesson on a high note
quiz.why: An effective conclusion retraces the important elements and relates them to the objective; new ideas, such as next lesson's material taught in detail, should not be introduced because they confuse learners [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]. Unrelated stories distract, even in the introduction [[25:112|AIH 5-9]].

quiz.q: Which kind of lecture lets learners take some part, and is the one aviation instructors favor?
options: Teaching lecture
Illustrated talk
Briefing
Formal lecture
quiz.why: The teaching lecture is planned so learners take some part, and aviation instructors favor it for that reason [[25:114|AIH 5-11]]. A formal lecture has little or no verbal participation, and a briefing is a concise array of facts [[25:114|AIH 5-11]].

quiz.q: Your lecture on IFR flight plans has run 25 minutes, and you see blank faces. What does the AIH say about retention, and what helps?
options: It peaks at about 20 minutes; push on to the summary
It holds steady if the slides are good; add more slides
It drops only for new pilots; seat them in front
It drops after 10-15 minutes; get learners involved
quiz.why: Retention drops off significantly after the first 10-15 minutes and improves at the end; adding active learner participation in the middle greatly increases it [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]. Better slides do not change that; the fix the AIH gives is active participation, since lectures do not give a precise measure of understanding [[25:116|AIH 5-13]].

quiz.q: Which is one of the AIH's conditions and controls for cooperative or group learning?
options: Large groups of learners with the same background
Individual accountability for each learner
Instructor answers held to the end of the task
Grades given only to the whole group, never individuals
quiz.why: Individual accountability is on the AIH's list, along with small, heterogeneous groups and recognition and rewards for group success [[25:124|AIH 5-21]]. Groups should be small and mixed, not large and alike [[25:124|AIH 5-21]].

quiz.q: You are leading a guided discussion on partial panel flying. Which is the better lead-off question?
options: Is partial panel flying harder than full panel flying?
Which instrument fails when the vacuum pump quits?
Did you cover the attitude indicator last flight?
Why does partial panel flying need a different scan?
quiz.why: Lead-off questions should usually begin with how or why so they start a discussion [[25:118|AIH 5-15]]. Avoid questions answered by yes or no or a short fact, like the other three [[25:117|AIH 5-14]].

quiz.q: What is an interim summary in a guided discussion?
options: A short summary after each learning outcome
A brief survey of the topic for unprepared learners
A quiz learners take at the midpoint of class
The notes learners hand in at the end of class
quiz.why: An interim summary usually follows the discussion of each learning outcome, bringing ideas together and helping the transition; it reinforces learning for that outcome [[25:118|AIH 5-15]]. A brief general survey in the introduction is the fix for learners with no prework [[25:118|AIH 5-15]].

quiz.q: This figure lists four phases of demonstration-performance, while Chapter 5 of the AIH lists five. Why the difference?
options: Chapter 9 drops evaluation for flight lessons
Chapter 9 moves the explanation to after the flight
Chapter 9 joins performance and supervision, done at once
Chapter 9 adds a review step and removes the demonstration
quiz.why: Chapter 5 lists explanation, demonstration, learner performance, instructor supervision and evaluation [[25:124|AIH 5-21]]. Chapter 9 combines performance and supervision because they are separate actions performed concurrently [[25:175|AIH 9-5]] [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. The explanation still comes before the flight [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

quiz.q: In the telling-and-doing technique, which step is the important transition the AIH points out?
options: Instructor tells, instructor does
Learner tells, instructor does
Learner tells, learner does
Learner does, instructor evaluates
quiz.why: The main difference from the demonstration-performance method is the transition learner tells, instructor does, between the second and third steps [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. In it the learner organizes the steps while you check understanding [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

quiz.q: The PTS item 'computer-based training' is closest to which term the current AIH text chooses to use?
options: Computer-assisted learning (CAL)
Web-based distance learning
Virtual reality (VR) training
Test preparation material
quiz.why: Of the many terms for the educational use of the computer, the AIH says it will use computer-assisted learning [[25:122|AIH 5-19]]; its glossary defines CBT as the use of the computer as a training device [[25:210|AIH G-2]]. Distance learning is one advantage of e-learning, not its name [[25:122|AIH 5-19]].

quiz.q: A learner wants to skip your holding ground lessons because an app covers them, then go fly holds. How does the AIH see that?
options: As a fine use of distance learning
As fine as long as the app tracks the scores
As improper or excessive e-learning
As fine once the knowledge test is passed
quiz.why: The AIH warns against relying only on a software program for ground instruction and then expecting the learner to perform in the aircraft [[25:122|AIH 5-19]]; learners who rely heavily on electronic media are generally not as well trained as those with a balanced mix [[25:172|AIH 9-2]]. Score tracking does not change that, since the computer cannot tell when a learner struggles [[25:122|AIH 5-19]].

quiz.q: Which is one of the AIH's traits of a good scenario?
options: It has one clearly right answer
It is a canned scenario for all
It promotes errors to debrief
It is not set up as a test
quiz.why: A good scenario is not a test, will not have one right answer, does not offer an obvious answer and should not promote errors [[25:120|AIH 5-17]]. There is no list of canned scenarios that can be used for all learners [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].

final_quiz.q: Your new instrument learner is a helicopter pilot adding an airplane instrument rating. What does the AIH say to do with that background when you plan blocks of learning?
options: Plan blocks that build on what the learner already knows
Start at block one, exactly as with any new learner
Skip the ground blocks and train only in the airplane
Ignore it, since helicopter time never transfers
final_quiz.why: Knowing the learner's background lets you plan blocks that build on what the learner already knows; the AIH's example is a helicopter pilot who understands speed control but not necessarily how to achieve it in an airplane [[25:147|AIH 7-3]]. Ground and flight should be integrated, not separated [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

final_quiz.q: In a lesson introduction, what is the motivation element for?
options: To give a road map of the objective and key ideas
To tell a joke that relaxes the class, on any topic
To give specific reasons the content matters
To test the learners on the previous lesson
final_quiz.why: Motivation gives specific reasons the lesson content is important, which ensures readiness [[25:112|AIH 5-9]]. The road map is the overview, and a joke unrelated to the subject distracts [[25:112|AIH 5-9]].

final_quiz.q: Which of these is a real limitation of the lecture method?
options: It cannot be used with large groups
It gives no precise measure of understanding
It cannot be used to present background information
It cannot be combined with other methods
final_quiz.why: Lectures do not give the instructor a precise measure of learner understanding [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]. They are convenient for large groups and well suited to background information [[25:116|AIH 5-13]], and they combine with other methods [[25:114|AIH 5-11]].

final_quiz.q: How should you deliver a teaching lecture on instrument approach charts?
options: Read it word for word so that nothing is missed
Memorize it and recite it from start to end
Keep notes hidden so learners trust you more
Speak from an outline, using notes openly
final_quiz.why: A good teaching lecture is extemporaneous: you speak from an outline and do not read or memorize it [[25:115|AIH 5-12]]. Use notes sparingly and unobtrusively, but make no effort to hide them [[25:115|AIH 5-12]].

final_quiz.q: After your lecture on IFR fuel planning, small groups solve the first problem together. What comes next in Bob's example?
options: The fastest group presents its answer, and class ends
You review the steps, then each learner solves one alone
You grade each group and record one score for all of them
Groups trade papers and grade each other's work
final_quiz.why: Bob reviews the steps used, then assigns another problem to be solved independently in class [[25:104|AIH 5-1]]. Before the performance phase ends, learners complete the task independently at least once [[25:125|AIH 5-22]].

final_quiz.q: Which result does the AIH report from research on cooperative learning?
options: Faster solo times and fewer flight hours
Lower cost per learner than a lecture
Less need for clear, specific objectives
Higher self-esteem and greater comprehension
final_quiz.why: Research indicates better test scores, higher self-esteem, improved social skills and greater comprehension [[25:124|AIH 5-21]]. Success still depends on clear, specific objectives [[25:124|AIH 5-21]].

final_quiz.q: Your instrument learner has grown in knowledge and experience. How does the AIH suggest the postflight guided discussion should change?
options: The learner leads it, guided by your questions
You lecture it so that nothing important is missed
You skip it and assign some reading on the errors
The learner fills in a written self-test, nothing more
final_quiz.why: As the learner grows in knowledge, the learner should be able to lead the postflight review while the instructor guides with targeted questions [[25:119|AIH 5-16]]. The goal of a guided discussion is to draw out the learner's knowledge, and the greater the participation, the more effective the learning [[25:116|AIH 5-13]].

final_quiz.q: During a guided discussion, a learner asks you a question. What does the AIH allow you to do?
options: Hold it until the conclusion to stay on time
Answer with a question, to the asker or another
Answer only yes or no to keep the group moving
Refer it to the reading to avoid a sidetrack
final_quiz.why: An instructor may answer a question with a question and direct it back to the person who asked or to another participant [[25:117|AIH 5-14]]. Yes or no answers do little to draw out knowledge, which is the goal [[25:116|AIH 5-13]].

final_quiz.q: While you demonstrate a level-off under the hood, turbulence makes the altitude wander from what you briefed. What should you do?
options: Say nothing, so the learner keeps confidence
Stop at once and let the learner try it
Acknowledge and explain the deviation now
Repeat the whole briefing before going on again
final_quiz.why: If the demonstration deviates from the explanation, the deviation should be immediately acknowledged and explained [[25:125|AIH 5-22]] [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. Learners imitate what they see, so an unexplained deviation can teach the wrong thing [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

final_quiz.q: In the learner tells, learner does step, what does the learner's thinking aloud let you find out?
options: Whether the learner prefers a visual style
Whether the learner has memorized every checklist item
Whether the airplane is trimmed for cruise
Whether an error is a misconception or a motor skill
final_quiz.why: Because the thinking is done verbally, it is easy to tell whether an error is induced by a misconception or a simple lack of motor skills [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. It also forces concentration on the task [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

final_quiz.q: The IFH describes an instructor demonstrating an excessive nose-down deviation followed by a large, hurried correction. What does that improper technique lead to?
options: A faster return to altitude, with no side effects
Overcontrolling and more extreme control inputs
A steady climb back with constant airspeed
Tumbling of the heading indicator's gyro
final_quiz.why: The normal impulse to make a large pitch correction in a hurry leads to overcontrolling, tension, erratic response and increasingly extreme control movements; the slower, smoother technique returns the airplane to the desired attitude more quickly [[23:165|IFH 7-4]].

final_quiz.q: An instrument applicant wants to credit 25 hours of instrument time from your school's FAA-approved AATD, with you instructing, toward the part 61 instrument rating. What applies?
options: All 25 hours count with an instructor present
AATD time cannot count toward instrument time
Up to 30 hours count under part 61 training
At most 20 hours in an AATD may be credited
final_quiz.why: A maximum of 20 hours in an advanced ATD may be credited, with an authorized instructor and FAA-approved tasks [[60:253|14 CFR 61.65(i)]]. The 30-hour figure applies to an FFS or FTD under part 142 [[60:252|14 CFR 61.65(h)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: In the AIH's integrated training curriculum for the ILS, what is the order?
options: Classroom knowledge, simulator practice, then the aircraft
The aircraft first, then the simulator, then the classroom
The simulator first, then the classroom, then the aircraft
The classroom, then the aircraft, then a simulator check
final_quiz.why: The instructor teaches ILS knowledge in the classroom, adds procedures and psychomotor practice in the simulator, and moves to the aircraft once the learner is proficient there [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]. The FAA recommends simulator training continue until tasks are accomplished successfully before trying them in the aircraft [[25:174|AIH 9-4]].

final_quiz.q: Why does the AIH want a flight scenario to begin with a reason to fly?
options: The ACS requires a trip purpose for every Task listed
A pilot's decisions change with the reason to fly
It keeps the learner from asking about the weather
It lets you skip the preflight briefing
final_quiz.why: A good scenario tells a story that begins with a reason to fly because a pilot's decisions differ depending on the motivation to fly [[25:120|AIH 5-17]]. The explanation and briefing still happen before the flight [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

final_quiz.q: Where does the AIH put maneuvers that need repetition in a scenario-based program?
options: They are dropped, since scenarios replace them
They wait until the practical test is passed
Concentrated practice first, then scenarios
They are taught only in devices, never in flight
final_quiz.why: SBT does not preclude maneuver-based training: maneuvers requiring repetition may still be taught in concentrated settings and, once learned, are integrated into realistic flight situations [[25:110|AIH 5-7]] [[25:154|AIH 7-10]].

final_quiz.q: In this SBT lesson plan, how does the postflight review typically begin?
options: With the learner's own self-critique
With the instructor's grade sheet
With a replay of the GPS track
With a quiz on the regulations
final_quiz.why: Figure 7-7 says the postflight discussion should typically begin with learner self-critique, with the instructor enabling the learner to solve the problems and draw conclusions [[25:156|AIH 7-12]]. Collaborative assessment pairs that self-assessment with the instructor's own [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

takeaways: All seven PTS items are in the current AIH; 'computer-based training' is now taught as e-learning and computer-assisted learning.
Organize every lesson as introduction (attention, motivation, overview), development by a clear pattern, and conclusion.
Lecture to give a group background fast, and break it up: retention drops after 10-15 minutes.
Group learning needs small mixed groups, clear objectives and individual accountability.
Guided discussion checks understanding with open how and why questions, and learners need background first.
Demonstration-performance (five phases in Chapter 5, four in Chapter 9) and telling-and-doing build skills: demonstrate exactly as it should be flown.
Computers and training devices are aids, not instructors: monitor progress, keep a balanced mix and know the credit limits.
SBT starts with a reason to fly, has no single right answer, and never allows an unsafe act.
cfi_notes: The AIH gives two phase counts for demonstration-performance: five in Chapter 5 and Figure 5-15 [[25:124|AIH 5-21]] [[25:125|AIH 5-22]], and four in Chapter 9 and Figure 9-6, where learner performance and instructor supervision are one concurrent phase [[25:175|AIH 9-5]] [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. Know both and say why they differ.

Naming: the PTS says 'computer-based training' [[FAA-S-8081-9E:24|PTS I.D]]. The 9B text uses e-learning and computer-assisted learning (CAL) [[25:121|AIH 5-18]] [[25:122|AIH 5-19]], its glossary treats CBT and CBI as synonyms [[25:210|AIH G-2]], and a separate glossary entry, computer-assisted instruction, means instruction in which the instructor is responsible for the class and uses the computer to assist [[25:210|AIH G-2]]. The text still uses 'computer-based training' in places, for example for setups with less instructor control [[25:130|AIH 5-27]] and in the levels of learning [[25:67|AIH 3-16]].

The same three-part structure has three sets of names: introduction, development and conclusion for a lesson plan [[25:112|AIH 5-9]]; introduction, body and summary for a lecture [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]; introduction, discussion and conclusion for a guided discussion [[25:117|AIH 5-14]].
The AIH gives two lists of what makes a good scenario: five traits on AIH 5-17 [[25:120|AIH 5-17]] and three on AIH 3-31 [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]. They do not conflict; give both if asked.

The IFH suggests demonstrating an improper pitch correction on purpose [[23:165|IFH 7-4]], while the AIH says to demonstrate exactly the way learners should practice, because they imitate the instructor [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Application: announce clearly that the first demonstration is the wrong way, and always finish with the correct one.

The PTS names only the guided discussion [[FAA-S-8081-9E:24|PTS I.D]]; the 9B also teaches a plain discussion method [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]. The glossary describes the guided discussion instructor as participating only as needed to keep the group focused [[25:211|AIH G-3]], while the text says the instructor maintains control [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]; both describe steering, not lecturing.

Device time: the AIH says there is no limit on how much time can be logged in an FFS, FTD or ATD, but credit is limited by parts 61 and 141 [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]. For the instrument rating, ATD credit is 10 hours (basic) or 20 hours (advanced), with a 20-hour total cap on device time except the part 142 case [[60:253|14 CFR 61.65(i)]] [[60:253|14 CFR 61.65(j)]].

How it is tested: per the PTS NOTE, the evaluator selects at least Tasks E, F and G and one other, so this Task may not come up [[FAA-S-8081-9E:23|PTS Area I NOTE]]. When it does, expect scenario-based questions that ask you to choose and justify a method for a learner, since the PTS asks evaluators to test application and correlation that way [[FAA-S-8081-9E:14|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]].
gaps: No source here gives a group size for cooperative learning; the AIH says only 'small, heterogeneous groups' [[25:124|AIH 5-21]].
No source says how long a lecture should run; the AIH gives only the retention drop after the first 10-15 minutes [[25:116|AIH 5-13]].
AC 61-136, which the AIH names for ATD approval and use [[25:173|AIH 9-3]], is not one of the build sources, so device-specific credits and letter of authorization details are not covered here.

No source gives ready-made instrument scenarios. The AIH says there is no list of canned scenarios for all learners [[25:82|AIH 3-31]], and the FAA generic syllabi and FITS material it mentions [[25:157|AIH 7-13]] are not build sources.
The PTS references FAA-H-8083-9; this lesson uses only the current 9B, so any older-edition material the 9B dropped is not covered.

activities.title: Which development pattern?
activities.intro: Tap an example, then the pattern of development it uses.

items.t: Trace radio navigation from the early systems to today
Teach Class D, E and G airspace before A, B and C
Normal landings before short-field and soft-field landings
Toy balloon forces before a gas turbine engine
The magnetic compass before gyroscopic heading indicators
Build on the speed control a helicopter pilot already knows
Basic navigation before a computerized navigation system

activities.why: Patterns and examples from [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]; normal before short-field and soft-field landings is the AIH's simple-to-complex example for blocks of learning [[25:146|AIH 7-2]]; building on a helicopter pilot's background [[25:147|AIH 7-3]].

activities.title: Kinds of lecture
activities.intro: Tap a kind of lecture or delivery, then what describes it.

pairs.r: Informs, persuades or entertains, little participation
Planned so learners take some part
Spoken from an outline, not read or memorized

activities.why: Kinds of lecture [[25:114|AIH 5-11]], extemporaneous delivery [[25:115|AIH 5-12]] and the informal lecture [[25:116|AIH 5-13]].

activities.title: True or false: group learning
activities.intro: Decide if each statement about cooperative or group learning is true or false.

cards.s: Groups should be small and made up of learners with similar backgrounds.
cards.why: False. The AIH calls for small, heterogeneous groups [[25:124|AIH 5-21]].

cards.s: Objectives should describe what each learner must be able to do on their own.
cards.why: True. Use clear, specific objectives for what learners acquire and then demonstrate on their own [[25:124|AIH 5-21]].

cards.s: Time to reflect on how the team worked together is part of the method.
cards.why: True. It is one of the AIH's conditions and controls [[25:124|AIH 5-21]].

cards.s: Once the groups form, the instructor should stay out of the way completely.
cards.why: False. The leader or instructor serves as a coach or facilitator, interacting as needed to keep the group on track and get everyone to take part [[25:124|AIH 5-21]].

cards.s: The AIH calls continual active participation perhaps its most significant characteristic.
Recognition for group success replaces individual accountability.
cards.why: False. Both are on the AIH's list [[25:124|AIH 5-21]].

activities.title: Run a guided discussion
activities.intro: Put the steps of a guided discussion in order, first to last, then tap Check.
steps: Assign background reading tied to the objective
Guide with how and why follow-up questions
Give an interim summary for that learning outcome
Conclude: summarize and tie the points to practical use
activities.why: Learners need background first; the discussion runs introduction, discussion and conclusion, with lead-off and follow-up questions, an interim summary after each outcome and a summary that ties points to practical application [[25:117|AIH 5-14]] [[25:118|AIH 5-15]].

activities.title: Which phase of demonstration-performance?
activities.intro: Tap an action, then the phase it belongs to (Chapter 9's four phases).

items.t: Brief objectives, standards and safety procedures before the flight
Invite questions on any step not understood
Show the maneuver with no extraneous activity
Acknowledge at once any departure from what you explained
The learner tries it right after the demonstration while you coach
Allot enough time for meaningful practice
The learner works alone while you judge it against how it was taught
Give concrete suggestions and avoid ending on a negative note

activities.title: True or false: computers and training devices
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: The AIH glossary treats computer-based training and computer-based instruction as the same thing.
cards.why: True. The terms and acronyms are synonymous [[25:210|AIH G-2]].

cards.s: With CAL you can step back, because the program spots learners who are struggling.
cards.why: False. The computer has no way of knowing when a learner is having difficulty; monitoring is always the instructor's job [[25:122|AIH 5-19]].

cards.s: An ATD with an FAA letter of authorization may be used for an instrument practical test.
cards.why: False. ATDs cannot be used for airman practical tests [[25:173|AIH 9-3]].

cards.s: The FAA recommends simulator training continue until tasks are done successfully, before trying them in the aircraft.
Learners who rely heavily on electronic media are generally as well trained as those given a balanced mix.
cards.why: False. They are generally not as well trained [[25:172|AIH 9-2]].

cards.s: Simulation and role-playing games usually promote critical thinking, but not every objective fits them.

activities.title: An instrument course, one method at a time
activities.intro: You are the CFII for Omar, a private pilot with 180 hours starting his instrument rating at a school with an FAA-approved AATD. He is your only learner. Pick the method for each step.

steps.s: First ground lesson: Omar needs the basics of how the flight instruments work and what each one tells him.
options: A cooperative group exercise with other learners
A short teaching lecture with questions, then a check of understanding
A scenario flight to an unfamiliar airport in marginal weather
Straight to the airplane to learn the instruments by doing
steps.why: A lecture suits background information [[25:116|AIH 5-13]], and learners need some subject knowledge before they can think beyond rote [[25:57|AIH 3-6]]. Group learning needs a group [[25:124|AIH 5-21]].

steps.s: Next: pitch control by reference to instruments.
options: An online module only, then on to approaches
A guided discussion only, since he already flies VFR
A case study of an accident, with no practice
Demonstration-performance in the AATD, then in the airplane
steps.why: Demonstration-performance is for skills that need practice [[25:124|AIH 5-21]], ground-based devices are valuable for the cross-check [[23:11|IFH viii]], and the FAA recommends simulator training until tasks are done successfully [[25:174|AIH 9-4]].

steps.s: In the AATD Omar makes big, hurried pitch corrections and overshoots the altitude.
options: Demonstrate the wrong and then the right correction, and have him talk his corrections aloud
Tell him to stop looking at the altimeter and fly by feel
Add a holding pattern so he is too busy to overcorrect
End the session and assign an online quiz on pitch
steps.why: The IFH contrasts the hurried correction with the slower, smoother one [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]; talking aloud shows whether the error is a misconception or motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

steps.s: After a partial panel lesson, and after Omar has done the IFH reading, you debrief.
options: A formal lecture listing every error you saw
A written test on partial panel facts only
A guided discussion with how and why questions he answers
No debrief, since the flight met the standards
steps.why: A guided discussion draws out what the learner knows and works in postflight briefings [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]; use open how and why questions [[25:117|AIH 5-14]]. Debriefing is necessary to motivate further progress [[23:342|IFH B-1]].

steps.s: Omar now flies approaches well. You want to build his IFR decision-making.
options: More approaches at the home airport until perfect
A scenario built on a real trip he wants to make, with planned changes
A lecture on aeronautical decision-making
A test-prep app with ADM questions
